name: Privacy-Enhancing Technologies
description: Systems and measurements for user privacy: tracking, anonymization, private data sharing, and privacy on the web/mobile.

uss.narrative:
The earliest work in this slice (USENIX 2018) is dominated by two threads: making sense of the opaque promises companies make about data, and the cat-and-mouse of web tracking. Polisis: Automated Analysis and Presentation of Privacy Policies Using Deep Learning (2018) used neural models to turn dense legal text into something users could actually query, while Unveiling and Quantifying Facebook Exploitation of Sensitive Personal Data for Advertising Purposes (2018) measured how platforms exploited sensitive categories under the new GDPR regime. In parallel, Fp-Scanner: The Privacy Implications of Browser Fingerprint Inconsistencies (2018) showed that the diversity of device configurations made browsers trackable even without cookies, setting up a defensive arms race.

Two big shifts follow. First, the policy-analysis line matures from reading policies to auditing whether apps obey them: PolicyLint: Investigating Internal Privacy Policy Contradictions on Google Play (2019) found policies that contradicted themselves, and Actions Speak Louder than Words: Entity-Sensitive Privacy Policy and Data Flow Analysis with PoliCheck (USENIX 2020) cross-checked stated promises against actual data flows. Second, the field discovers that privacy threats are deeply human and physical, not just abstract. Clinical Computer Security for Victims of Intimate Partner Violence (2019) and the follow-on study The Tools and Tactics Used in Intimate Partner Surveillance (2020) reframed privacy around at-risk users facing targeted, persistent surveillance, while a wave of sensing-era papers (You Are What You Broadcast, 2020; Kalεido, 2021; Lumos, 2022) tackled privacy leaking through WiFi, eye-tracking, and hidden cameras in physical spaces.

A defining breakthrough of this period is protective perturbation against machine learning. Fawkes: Protecting Privacy against Unauthorized Deep Learning Models (USENIX 2020) cloaked photos to defeat facial-recognition scrapers like Clearview, and the same lineage extended to creators with Glaze: Protecting Artists from Style Mimicry by Text-to-Image Models (USENIX 2023), responding directly to diffusion models like Stable Diffusion. Alongside this, the cryptographic toolbox for private computation grew sharply: Pancake: Frequency Smoothing for Encrypted Data Stores (2020), private set intersection and union work (Fuzzy Labeled PSI, 2021; Linear Private Set Union, 2023), and PIR advances (Constant-weight PIR, 2022) moved from theory toward deployable private data sharing, including hard problems like detecting harmful media under end-to-end encryption (2021).

Where it stands now: the agenda has broadened from web tracking into regulation-aware auditing, protocol design, and applied cryptography. Recent work automates compliance at web scale (Automating Cookie Consent and GDPR Violation Detection, 2022; Leaky Forms, 2022), hardens core infrastructure (Privacy-Preserving and Standard-Compatible AKA Protocol for 5G, 2021), and pushes formal privacy into data publication (PrivGraph: Differentially Private Graph Data Publication, 2023). Meanwhile the fingerprinting arms race never ended, migrating to extensions and Tor traffic (Online Website Fingerprinting, 2022). The throughline across venues is a maturation from measuring and exposing privacy harms toward building practical, deployable defenses for real users, regulators, and at-risk populations.

ndss.narrative:
The earliest work in this collection, all from NDSS 2018, treated privacy as an empirical measurement problem: go look at what real systems leak, at scale. "Apps, Trackers, Privacy, and Regulators: A Global Study of the Mobile Tracking Ecosystem" (NDSS 2018) mapped the sprawling third-party tracking economy embedded in mobile apps, while "Bug Fixes, Improvements, ... and Privacy Leaks" (NDSS 2018) followed PII leaks across app versions over time. Alongside these ecosystem studies ran a parallel thread on de-anonymization — showing that supposedly anonymous data betrays identity, whether from "De-anonymization of Mobility Trajectories" (NDSS 2018) or even from compiled code in "When Coding Style Survives Compilation: De-anonymizing Programmers from Executable Binaries" (NDSS 2018).

Over 2019-2020 the attacks pushed into new layers of the stack. Researchers moved below the app into the cellular network, with "GUTI Reallocation Demystified" (NDSS 2018) and then "Privacy Attacks to the 4G and 5G Cellular Paging Protocols Using Side Channel Information" (NDSS 2019) showing that temporary identifiers and paging messages still leak location. The web-tracking arms race intensified through browser-extension fingerprinting in "Carnus" (NDSS 2020) and side channels like "DNS Cache-Based User Tracking" (NDSS 2019). A distinctive new front opened on connected devices: "Packet-Level Signatures for Smart Home Devices" (NDSS 2020) showed that encrypted smart-home traffic still reveals what you are doing, a theme that "PFirewall" (NDSS 2021) then tried to defend. This period also saw genomic and biomedical privacy arrive, from "MBeacon" (NDSS 2019) to "Genotype Extraction and False Relative Attacks" (NDSS 2020).

By the early 2020s two things stood out: fingerprinting kept getting more physical, and defenses matured alongside the attacks. "DRAWN APART: A Device Identification Technique based on Remote GPU Fingerprinting" (NDSS 2022) reached down to hardware manufacturing variation to tell identical devices apart, while "Tales of Favicons and Caches" (NDSS 2021) showed tracking persisting through the very caches meant to be harmless. On the defensive and cryptographic side, work like "Obfuscated Access and Search Patterns in Searchable Encryption" (NDSS 2021), "OBI: a multi-path oblivious RAM" (NDSS 2023), and "AAKA: An Anti-Tracking Cellular Authentication Scheme" (NDSS 2024) turned earlier attack findings into concrete protections.

The most recent work, clustered in NDSS 2026, shows the area absorbing the LLM era while its classic problems persist. "Prεεmpt: Sanitizing Sensitive Prompts for LLMs" (NDSS 2026) and "ExpShield: Safeguarding Web Text from Unauthorized Crawling and LLM Exploitation" (NDSS 2026) confront a new privacy adversary — the model itself and the crawlers that feed it. At the same time the old threads run on: "Cross-Boundary Mobile Tracking" (NDSS 2026) revisits mobile tracking inside Android WebViews, "WiFinger" (NDSS 2026) continues the IoT traffic-fingerprinting line begun in 2020, "Lightening the Load" (NDSS 2026) advances provable website-fingerprinting defenses, and large-scale measurement lives on in "Hey there! You are using WhatsApp: Enumerating Three Billion Accounts" (NDSS 2026). Cryptographic privacy also keeps maturing, with FHE-based analytics in "Select-Then-Compute" (NDSS 2026). The field today is a two-sided contest — measurement and attacks constantly finding new leaks across mobile, cellular, IoT, and now AI systems, met by increasingly practical anonymization, encryption, and anti-tracking defenses.

sp.narrative:
The earliest work in this collection, all from IEEE S&P 2018, already spans the two poles that would define the area. On one side sits heavy cryptographic machinery for private data access, exemplified by "PIR with Compressed Queries and Amortized Query Processing" (S&P 2018), which worked to make private information retrieval affordable, and by "Oblix: An Efficient Oblivious Search Index" (S&P 2018). On the other side sits empirical measurement of how users actually leak information: "FP-STALKER: Tracking Browser Fingerprint Evolutions" (S&P 2018) showed fingerprints could be linked over time, while "Speechless" (S&P 2018) and "When Your Fitness Tracker Betrays You" (S&P 2018) revealed sensors as covert side channels. A parallel thread questioned the encryption meant to protect us, with "Improved Reconstruction Attacks on Encrypted Data Using Range Query Leakage" (S&P 2018) opening a sustained assault on searchable encryption.

That leakage-abuse thread matured quickly. "Learning to Reconstruct" (S&P 2019) recast database reconstruction as a statistical learning problem, and follow-ups on k-nearest-neighbor leakage (S&P 2019) and non-uniform query distributions in "The State of the Uniform" (S&P 2020) hardened the attacks against realistic assumptions. Meanwhile the tracking-and-defense arms race intensified on the web: "SensorID" (S&P 2019) fingerprinted phones through calibration data, "AdGraph" (S&P 2020) brought graph-based ad and tracker blocking, and "Do Cookie Banners Respect my Choice?" (S&P 2020) turned GDPR compliance into a measurement study. By "Fingerprinting the Fingerprinters" (S&P 2021), the community had inverted the problem, learning to detect trackers automatically. A distinct differential-privacy line also emerged here, from "PrivKV" (S&P 2019) collecting key-value data under local DP to "Lightweight Techniques for Private Heavy Hitters" (S&P 2021).

The early 2020s broadened both the threat surface and the cryptographic toolkit. Physical-layer privacy became a topic in its own right, with "IRShield" (S&P 2022) defending against wireless sensing and "Evaluating Physical-Layer BLE Location Tracking Attacks" (S&P 2022) measuring beacon tracking, while "Surakav" (S&P 2022) and the sobering "SoK: A Critical Evaluation of Efficient Website Fingerprinting Defenses" (S&P 2023) fought the traffic-analysis battle. Privacy-preserving cryptography grew more practical and deployable: "zk-creds" (S&P 2023) built anonymous credentials on existing identity documents via zkSNARKs, "Threshold BBS+ Signatures" (S&P 2023) distributed credential issuance, and blockchain privacy advanced from "A2L" (S&P 2021) through "BlindHub" (S&P 2023). "Flamingo" (S&P 2023) pushed secure aggregation toward private federated learning, and "SoK: Privacy-Preserving Data Synthesis" (S&P 2024) took stock of synthetic-data methods.

The most recent work, dominated by S&P 2026, shows a field pulling in two directions at once. The cryptographic core keeps refining its foundations, with "Piano" (S&P 2024) achieving simple single-server sublinear PIR and 2026 entries like "Single-Server Stateful PIR with Verifiability", "ZELDA: Efficient Multi-Server Preprocessing PIR", "Practical Multi-Party Private Set Intersection", "Jigsaw: Doubly Private Smart Contracts", and "Blinding Post-Quantum Hash-and-Sign Signatures" extending PIR, PSI, private contracts, and blind signatures into post-quantum and verifiable regimes. At the same time the human- and systems-facing side is turning to AI and everyday deployments: "Navigating Developers' Quagmire" (S&P 2026) uses LLMs to audit SDK privacy compliance, "Your Eyes Won't Lie" (S&P 2026) snoops voting privacy through webcams, and "Privacy Perspectives and Practices of Chinese Smart Home Product Teams" (S&P 2026) studies the developers who build privacy in or leave it out. The area has thus moved from foundational attacks and building blocks toward a mature ecosystem that pairs post-quantum-ready cryptography with LLM-assisted, developer-centered privacy governance.

ccs.narrative:
Privacy-enhancing technologies at CCS span measurement studies, system designs, and formal mechanisms. The 2018-2019 period was anchored by tracking and consent: (Un)informed Consent: Studying GDPR Consent Notices in the Field (CCS 2019) conducted the first large-scale field study of cookie consent notices, revealing systematic dark patterns and fatigue. Simultaneously, searchable encryption research produced Practical Backward-Secure Searchable Encryption from Symmetric Puncturable Encryption (CCS 2018) and Result Pattern Hiding Searchable Encryption for Conjunctive Queries (CCS 2018), which tackled server-side leakage in cloud storage.

Website fingerprinting as a privacy threat to Tor users became a sustained research thread, starting with Deep Fingerprinting (CCS 2018), countered by TrafficSliver: Fighting Website Fingerprinting Attacks with Traffic Splitting (CCS 2020), and later revisited with Realistic Website Fingerprinting By Augmenting Network Traces (CCS 2023). Location privacy received formal treatment through Utility-Aware Synthesis of Differentially Private and Attack-Resilient Location Traces (CCS 2018).

The 2020-2024 period saw PETs applied to machine learning pipelines. Analyzing Information Leakage of Updates to Natural Language Models (CCS 2020) showed model-update differencing leaks training data, and DP-Forward: Fine-tuning and Inference on Language Models with Differential Privacy in Forward Pass (CCS 2023) proposed a forward-pass DP mechanism for LLM fine-tuning and inference.

milestones.title: Practical Backward-Secure Searchable Encryption from Symmetric Puncturable Encryption
milestones.note: Made backward privacy achievable in practice using symmetric puncturable encryption, closing a key leakage gap.

milestones.title: Result Pattern Hiding Searchable Encryption for Conjunctive Queries
milestones.note: Hid both access and result patterns for conjunctive queries, advancing the strongest searchable encryption security goals.

milestones.title: Utility-Aware Synthesis of Differentially Private and Attack-Resilient Location Traces
milestones.note: Synthesized location traces under DP that remain useful while resisting known inference attacks.

milestones.title: (Un)informed Consent: Studying GDPR Consent Notices in the Field
milestones.note: Landmark empirical study exposing that GDPR consent dialogs routinely use dark patterns and fail user comprehension.

milestones.title: Triplet Fingerprinting: More Practical and Portable Website Fingerprinting with N-shot Learning
milestones.note: Made website fingerprinting attacks on Tor practical with very few training examples via N-shot learning.

milestones.title: TrafficSliver: Fighting Website Fingerprinting Attacks with Traffic Splitting
milestones.note: Proposed traffic splitting across Tor entry paths as a practical, low-overhead fingerprinting defense.

milestones.title: Analyzing Information Leakage of Updates to Natural Language Models
milestones.note: Showed that differencing consecutive model snapshots recovers information about training data changes.

milestones.title: DP-Forward: Fine-tuning and Inference on Language Models with Differential Privacy in Forward Pass
milestones.note: Applied DP to the forward pass of LLMs to protect against embedding-level inference attacks at fine-tuning and inference time.

top4.narrative:
The earliest work in this set, from 2018, already spans the two poles that still define privacy-enhancing technologies: understanding how data is actually collected, and building cryptographic machinery to prevent that collection. On the measurement side, Polisis (USENIX 2018) used deep learning to parse the privacy policies companies write but few users read, while Apps, Trackers, Privacy, and Regulators (NDSS 2018) mapped the sprawling mobile third-party tracking ecosystem and FP-STALKER (S&P 2018) tracked how browser fingerprints evolve to follow users without cookies. On the cryptographic side, PIR with Compressed Queries (S&P 2018) and Oblix (S&P 2018) pushed private retrieval and oblivious search toward practicality — but Improved Reconstruction Attacks on Encrypted Data (S&P 2018) simultaneously showed that access-pattern and range-query leakage can reconstruct supposedly encrypted databases, launching a long cat-and-mouse thread.

Two forces reshaped the area around 2019-2020. First, GDPR turned regulation into a measurable object: (Un)informed Consent (CCS 2019) and Do Cookie Banners Respect my Choice? (S&P 2020) quantified how poorly consent notices comply in practice, while PolicyLint (USENIX 2019) and PoliCheck (USENIX 2020) automated the detection of contradictions between what apps promise and what they do. Second, the leakage-attack thread matured into a science — Learning to Reconstruct (S&P 2019) tied database reconstruction to statistical learning theory, prompting volume-hiding defenses (CCS 2019) — even as differential privacy moved from theory to deployed data collection through PrivKV (S&P 2019), private location traces (CCS 2018), the shuffle model (CCS 2020), and private heavy hitters (S&P 2021). A striking new direction was user-side cloaking: Fawkes (USENIX 2020) weaponized adversarial perturbations so ordinary people could poison unauthorized facial-recognition models.

By the early-to-mid 2020s the field had branched into concrete, deployable defenses and detection. Fingerprinting the Fingerprinters (S&P 2021) turned years of tracking measurement into automated script detection; website-fingerprinting research moved from lab conditions toward realistic settings with Zero-delay Lightweight Defenses (USENIX 2020) and Online Website Fingerprinting (USENIX 2022); smart-home traffic analysis surfaced with Packet-Level Signatures (NDSS 2020). The cloaking idea from Fawkes was carried into the generative-AI era by Glaze (USENIX 2023), which shields artists from style mimicry, and anonymous-credential systems became practical and web-deployable with zk-creds (S&P 2023) building on zkSNARKs and existing identity infrastructure.

The most recent work, clustered in the 2026 NDSS cohort, shows the frontier moving in two directions at once. Privacy measurement has gone to platform scale and across app boundaries: Hey there! You are using WhatsApp (NDSS 2026) enumerated roughly three billion accounts, Connecting the Dots (NDSS 2026) links private user data across messaging apps, Cross-Boundary Mobile Tracking (NDSS 2026) exposes Java-to-JavaScript leakage inside Android WebViews, and WiFinger (NDSS 2026) fingerprints noisy IoT event traffic. Meanwhile the classic threads persist and adapt to LLMs — Learning from Leakage (NDSS 2026) revives database reconstruction from just a few range queries, Lightening the Load (NDSS 2026) offers a provable website-fingerprinting defense, and a new LLM-privacy subfield emerges with Preempt (NDSS 2026) sanitizing sensitive prompts and ExpShield (NDSS 2026) safeguarding web text from unauthorized crawling and model exploitation. The through-line from 2018 holds: measure how data actually leaks, then engineer defenses that survive real-world adversaries.
